newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria debates jobs, right targets foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Austria debates jobs, right targets foreigners.

text.p: Austria's parliament began an emergency debate on the nation's record unemployment on Tuesday as pressure groups warned against making scapegoats of foreign workers.

The opposition, far-right Freedom Party called the debate earlier this month when it emerged January unemployment had breached the magic 300,000 level for the first time since World War Two and the founding of the Second Republic.

Party leader Joerg Haider is urging the government of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party to clamp down on immigration and encourage unemployed foreigners to return home. He also argues that a lighter tax burden on small and medium-sized firms would stimulate job creation.
"300,000 foreign workers are too many when we have 300,000 unemployed," Haider told a news conference ahead of the debate.
"It is not about sending working foreigners home but about securing social peace for those foreigners who have lived and worked in Austria for a long time."
Around a dozen activists from pressure group SOS Mitmensch protested in front of parliament as the session began. They wore t-shirts with the slogan "scapegoats".
"The number of foreigners in Austria and the level of unemployment are two completely separate issues," said spokesman Martin Schenk.

There were signs, however, that some of Haider's arguments had struck a chord with the government of Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima, aware how mass unemployment sparked social unrest in the 1930s.
Klima, who took over from Franz Vranitzky in January, has said he is open to suggestions from all political quarters, including the Freedom Party, and ousted left-wingers from key cabinet posts.

New Interior Minister Karl Schloegl has already said he wants to stem the influx of foreigners joining their families in Austria, a clear departure from the policies of his more liberal predecessor Caspar Einem.
"We cannot allow family members to enter the country in the numbers foreseen by my predecessor," Schloegl said in a newspaper interview.
He forecast that the 1998 quota for family members would be well below this year's 10,000.

The People's Party, junior partner in the coalition government, has added its voice to the calls for strict immigration controls. Whip Andreas Khol said he wanted to see a foreigner quota of 4,000 in 1998, down from 17,320 this year.
In a speech at the start of Tuesday's debate, Klima said there was no easy solution to the thorny problem of unemployment but he vowed the government would do its utmost to create new jobs.
He praised employers and unions for striking a landmark deal on flexible working hours and said the agreement would boost Austrian competitiveness in international markets.

The deal, reached on Monday night after months of talks, extends the working week to a maximum 50 hours during busy periods from a rigid 38-40 hours at present. Workers will take time off in lieu during slack spells.
Haider slammed the move. "The first concrete measure of the new Klima government means a loss of income to workers. Flexibility has been achieved at the expense of ordinary people," he said.
